open-question.question: Beyond refusing an empty title or body, does the task-list tool validate an authored section against task-format.md (title of 4 to 8 title-cased words, a 1 to 3 sentence body, no sub-heading or labeled section inside the body), or does it accept any body text as the section's prose and leave the format to the authoring skills?
open-question.alternative: The insert and append subcommands refuse, with one Error: line and the files unchanged, only a title or body that would break the tool's own parse: a title holding a line break, and a body holding a line that the parser reads as a section boundary (a bare `---` line or a line opening with `## `). Everything else — heading lines at other levels, labeled sections, title length and case, sentence count — is accepted as prose and left to the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Guarantees that every section the tool writes is parsed back as exactly that section, which is the property a sole writer exists to secure, while keeping the tool free of any authoring rule, so task-format.md stays the only home of the format and no brief is refused for its wording. The ban on sub-headings and labeled sections, the property task altitude protects most directly, stays prose-only, so a `**Steps:**` block or a `### Notes` heading inside a body is still written without complaint.

Beyond refusing an empty title or body, the insert and append subcommands write whatever title and body they are given verbatim, including a body line that reads as a `---` separator or a `## ` heading; the move copies its section as it stands. Every rule in task-format.md, structural or quantitative, stays with the authoring skills exactly as today, and the tool checks none of it. The smallest tool and the simplest contract: the tool is a pure writer with no format knowledge, task-format.md stays the single home of the format, and no authored brief is ever refused for its wording, so a headless derive or submit run never stops on a format judgment. The tool can write a file its own parser then splits differently (a body holding a `---` line becomes two sections and the next move slices it wrongly), so the sole writer does not guarantee the shape it parses; and the format rules stay unenforced, as they are today.

The insert and append subcommands refuse the parse-breaking title or body of the integrity guard and, in addition, any body line that opens a sub-heading (a line opening with `#` at any level) or a labeled section (a line that is a bold label ending in a colon, such as `**Steps:**`, `**Notes:**`, or `**Verified:**`). Title length, title case, and sentence count are not checked and stay with the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Enforces mechanically, with deterministic line-level tests that need no heuristic, the one rule whose breach changes a task's altitude (no steps, notes, success, or Verified section in an authored brief), and keeps a `**Verified:**` label out of TASKS_TODO.md where it would confuse the completion bar. Puts a second statement of part of the format in the tool, so a later change to task-format.md's structural rule must be mirrored in code and tests; and a body that legitimately quotes a bold-labelled phrase on its own line is refused.

The insert and append subcommands refuse everything the structural checks refuse and, in addition, a title whose whitespace-split word count falls outside 4 to 8. Title case and the 1 to 3 sentence count are not checked, because neither has an unambiguous mechanical test, and stay with the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Enforces every rule of task-format.md that has a deterministic test and no other, so the tool never refuses on a heuristic misjudgment, while a title too short to be unique or too long to be a handle is stopped at write time. The numeric title bound now lives in task-format.md and in the tool and must be kept in step by hand; and the body length, the rule most often stretched in practice, stays unenforced.

The insert and append subcommands refuse every rule of task-format.md they can test: the parse-breaking and structural lines above, a title outside 4 to 8 words, a title that is not title-cased by a fixed rule the tool defines (for example every word opening with a capital or a non-letter), and a body whose counted sentences fall outside 1 to 3 by a fixed counting rule the tool defines (for example sentence-ending punctuation followed by whitespace or the end of the body, outside code spans). There is no override; the move copies its section as it stands. The tool becomes the complete enforcement point of the task format, so no runner, headless or not, can write a brief that drifts from the template, and the format rules gain the tests the authoring prose never had. The sentence count and title-case tests are heuristics (abbreviations such as `e.g.`, file names, decimals, and minor words in titles all misfire), so legitimate briefs are refused and a headless derive or submit run stops on a false positive; one milestone-41 brief already holds four sentences by a naive count, and the format's numbers gain a second home in the tool.

The insert and append subcommands run the full set of checks of the full format refusal by default, but accept a flag (for example `--allow-format`) under which the length, case, and sentence-count checks are skipped while the parse-breaking and structural checks still apply; the authoring skills pass the flag only after re-reading a refused brief and judging the breach deliberate. The move copies its section as it stands. Keeps the full format enforced by default while giving a runner a deliberate way past a heuristic false positive, so a legitimate four-sentence brief is written rather than mangled to satisfy a counter. Adds a flag and a refusal-then-retry turn to the authoring skills' prose, and a flag a runner may pass reflexively erodes the check it exists to soften; the format's numbers still gain a second home in the tool.

The insert and append subcommands enforce only the parse-integrity guard and otherwise write the section as given; the tool gains a separate read-only subcommand (for example `check`) that reports, one line per finding in the read contract's bare-value style, every section of a task file breaching a structural, title-length, title-case, or sentence-count rule of task-format.md, which an authoring skill may run after writing and a reviewer may run at any time. Nothing is refused for format. Gives the format a mechanical check, heuristics included, without ever blocking a write on a false positive, and keeps every mutator's "prints nothing on success" contract intact. A check nobody is required to act on can be skipped or ignored, so the format is no more enforced than today unless the authoring prose adds a step to run it and react, which costs a tool call and turn per run; and it adds a subcommand and a second home for the format's numbers.

The insert and append subcommands enforce only the parse-integrity guard as a refusal, and for every structural, title-length, title-case, or sentence-count breach of task-format.md still write the section but print one warning line per breach on stderr and exit 0. Nothing is refused for format; the move copies its section as it stands. The runner sees each format breach in the very call that wrote the section, with no extra subcommand or turn, and no heuristic misfire ever blocks a write. Breaks the shared tool contract that a mutator prints nothing on success, so callers and tests can no longer read any stderr output as failure, and a warning arriving after the write leaves the runner either to ignore it or to spend a further call correcting a section already on disk.

open-question.question: When the task-list tool is given a task title (the section to move, or a before/after anchor), does it match it exactly after whitespace- and case-folding, refusing anything else so a partial task name is resolved by the runner's own read of TASKS_TODO.md before the call, or does it carry the completion procedure's case-insensitive partial match itself, which then needs a rule for two sections matching and a way to tell the runner which heading it took?
open-question.recommendation: The tool keeps the open-question tool's folded-id comparison and silent-mutator contract while the partial-name convenience survives at no cost in step 1's whole read, which complete-all-tasks already bypasses by passing the exact heading; the tool-side partial forms resolve the name twice by two rules and two of them break the silent-mutator contract, and retiring the convenience widens the milestone for a problem the runner's read already solves.
open-question.alternative: The tool matches every title it is given (the section to move and a before/after anchor alike) against the `##` headings only by exact equality after whitespace-folding and case-folding, the open-question tool's id comparison; anything else, a partial name or two sections sharing the folded title included, is refused with one Error: line and both files unchanged. The completion procedure keeps its case-insensitive partial match in prose: step 1 resolves the user's partial name against its own whole read of TASKS_TODO.md (listing the headings on no match, as today) and the runner passes the full heading it located to the move. The tool prints nothing on success. Keeps the tool deterministic and its contract identical to open_questions.py (folded ids, silent mutator, one Error: line), while the partial-name convenience the inline /complete-task documents survives at no extra cost, since step 1 already reads TASKS_TODO.md whole and complete-all-tasks already passes the exact heading. Name resolution is split between prose and tool, so the runner must copy the located heading verbatim into the call and a heading it retypes differently in more than case or whitespace is refused after the work is done; a duplicated folded title in the file blocks the move entirely, which leans on title uniqueness, a condition the uniqueness-enforcement question owns.

The tool matches a title only when it equals a `##` heading's text byte for byte after trimming the line's ends, with no case- or inner-whitespace-folding, and refuses anything else with one Error: line and both files unchanged. The completion procedure keeps its partial match in prose and passes the exact heading it located; the tool prints nothing on success. The strictest and simplest rule: the title the tool matched is exactly the text that lands in the Task-completion: subject and in TASKS_DONE.md, with no comparison form to define or test. Breaks parity with the open-question tool's folded-id convention, so the workflow's two sole-writer tools compare titles differently, and a runner's harmless case or spacing slip in retyping a heading becomes a refused move.

The tool matches by exact equality after whitespace- and case-folding and refuses anything else, as in the first option, and the partial match is retired from the workflow altogether: complete-procedure.md step 1 also requires the given name to equal a heading after folding, the inline /complete-task's "full or partial text" argument contract becomes full text only, and a no-match still stops listing the available headings so the caller can retry. The tool prints nothing on success. One matching rule from the user's argument through step 1 to the tool, so the section the procedure read and the section the tool moves can never diverge, and the prose loses its loosest rule rather than merely relocating it. Takes away a documented convenience of the inline skill (typing a fragment of a long title) and widens the milestone's prose and doc edits to the skill's argument contract and docs/skill-reference.md, for a matching problem the runner's own read already solves.

alternative.id: Tool partial, refuse ambiguity, print heading

open-question.alternative: The tool carries the matching itself for the moved section and the anchors alike: an exact folded match wins when one exists, otherwise a case-insensitive substring match against the headings must be unique; two or more partial matches are refused with one Error: line naming the candidate headings and both files unchanged. On success the move prints the full heading it took on stdout, an exception to the rule that a mutator prints nothing, so the runner can use it in the commit subject. The completion procedure passes the user's name as given. Matching moves out of prose into tested code with a defined ambiguity rule, and the runner learns authoritatively which heading moved, so the subject and report cannot name a different task than the files record. Breaks the silent-mutator contract both existing tools hold, and step 1 still has to locate and read the section in prose before the work, so the name is resolved twice (prose at step 1, tool at step 5) by two rules that can disagree; a partial anchor can also land a submitted task beside the wrong section.

The tool carries the same exact-first, then unique case-insensitive substring match for the moved section and the anchors alike, refusing two or more partial matches with one Error: line naming the candidates and both files unchanged, and it prints nothing on success; the runner takes the heading for its commit subject and report from its own step-1 read of the section. Gains a tested, defined ambiguity rule in the tool while keeping the silent-mutator contract both existing tools share. The heading the runner reports comes from its prose read, not from the tool, so a disagreement between the prose resolution at step 1 and the tool's resolution at step 5 goes unseen, and the tool's partial matching duplicates work the runner has already done.

alternative.id: Tool partial, first match, print heading

open-question.alternative: The tool carries the matching for the moved section and the anchors alike: an exact folded match wins when one exists, otherwise the first heading in file order containing the name case-insensitively is taken, with no ambiguity refusal; on success the move prints the full heading it took on stdout so the runner can name it. Never refuses a name that matches something, mirroring the unstated first-hit behaviour runners exhibit today, and the printed heading tells the runner what was moved. A fragment shared by two titles silently moves or anchors on whichever comes first, and the runner learns of a wrong pick only after both task files have changed; it also breaks the silent-mutator contract.

alternative.id: Partial for move, exact for anchors

open-question.alternative: The rule differs by argument: the moved section's title is matched by the tool exact-first, then by a unique case-insensitive substring, two or more partial matches refused with one Error: line naming the candidates, while a before/after anchor is matched only by exact whitespace- and case-folded equality. The tool prints nothing on success and the runner takes the moved heading from its own step-1 read. Puts partial matching only where a human-typed name reaches the tool (the /complete-task argument) and keeps anchors, which submit-task chooses from its own read of the file, strict so an insert never lands beside a guessed section. Two matching rules in one tool for the same kind of value make its contract harder to state and test, and the move still resolves its name twice (prose and tool); how an anchor naming no section is handled stays a condition the unknown-anchor question owns.

open-question.question: Does the task-list tool parse a whole task file and re-render it in one canonical layout on every write, normalizing the blank-line convention of every section it did not touch, or does it splice only the bytes of the section it adds or removes and leave every other byte of the file as it stands?
open-question.alternative: On every write (initialize, append, insert, move) the tool parses the whole task file into its heading line and its ## sections (title, body prose, and for a done entry the **Verified:** bullets), applies the change to that model, and renders the entire file in one canonical layout: a blank line after the heading, after the body, after the label, after the last bullet, after each ---, and the file ending in --- plus one newline. Every section the call did not touch is re-emitted in that layout too, so any blank-line drift in it is normalized silently on the first write; the body prose itself is carried through as parsed text. The file is replaced through the same-directory temporary file, as open_questions.py does. One write path that mirrors open_questions.py's render-then-replace, so output is deterministic and testable against golden fixtures, and the seam failures runners hit today (a milestone-45 agent ran a second script to restore the blank line between a --- and the next heading) cannot occur anywhere in the file, which converges on the documented convention after one write. The first write to a file that drifted (milestone_41 ends in an extra blank line, milestone_42 holds a double blank, milestone_30 lacks a blank after a separator) or that someone edited by hand rewrites sections the commit is not about, so the Task-completion or Task-submission diff carries unrelated whitespace churn; and the parser must round-trip every body shape (internal paragraph breaks, lists, fenced code with blank lines) or it alters content it was never asked to touch. How strict that parse is depends on the unterminated-section and format-validation axes the sibling questions own.

The tool parses and renders the whole file in the one canonical layout, as above, but before writing it re-renders the file as read and compares it to the bytes on disk: if the two differ, the call is refused with one Error: line naming the file and the files are left unchanged; only a file already in canonical form is written, through the same render-then-replace path. Initialization, which replaces the contents by design, is the one write not gated on the old bytes. Keeps the single deterministic render path and its testability while guaranteeing the tool never silently changes a byte of a section it was not asked to touch, so every task commit's diff is exactly the change made, and drift is surfaced the moment it appears instead of being absorbed. Any hand edit or historical drift that is not byte-canonical blocks every subsequent tool call on that file until someone fixes it by hand, which stops a headless complete-all-tasks run mid-milestone on a cosmetic difference; and body text the parser cannot round-trip exactly becomes a refusal rather than a write, so the parser's fidelity is load-bearing for availability.

The tool parses only to locate boundaries (the target section's ## line through its ---, or the anchor's position) and writes by splicing: a removal deletes exactly that byte span, an insertion or append places a canonically rendered new section at the located offset, and every other byte of the file, including the whitespace around the splice point, stays as it stands. No section, separator, or blank line outside the inserted or removed span is rewritten; the file is still replaced atomically through a same-directory temporary file. The tool changes nothing it was not asked to change, so diffs are minimal, hand-edited or drifted sections survive untouched, and the parser need only find headings and separators rather than model and round-trip every body shape. The new section inherits whatever whitespace its neighbour leaves, so a neighbour missing its trailing blank line yields a heading jammed against a --- (the exact repair a milestone-45 agent had to script), and removing a section can leave a double blank or none; layout consistency is not guaranteed, drift accumulates, and tests must cover splice offsets rather than one rendered form. Locating boundaries still depends on how the unterminated-section sibling resolves a section with no ---.

The tool keeps every byte of every untouched section exactly as it stands, as in a pure splice, but normalizes the whitespace at each junction its own write creates: an inserted or appended section gets exactly one blank line before its ## heading and one after its ---, and the gap a removed section leaves collapses to the single blank line the convention calls for, with the end of file normalized to --- plus one newline only when the write touched the end. Drift anywhere away from a junction is left in place. Combines a minimal diff and no silent rewriting of other sections with a guarantee that every seam the tool produces is well-formed, so the jammed-heading and doubled-blank failures cannot be introduced by a write even into a drifted file. It is a third behaviour with its own rules to specify and test (which whitespace counts as part of a seam, what happens at the file heading and at end of file), more logic than either a render or a raw splice, and it still leaves the file internally inconsistent wherever drift sits away from a junction, so the file never converges on the convention by itself.

open-question.question: Inside its one shell call, does derive-tasks write its ordered briefs as one tool process per brief (each brief its own quoted heredoc, refused alone while the rest land), or as one tool process that takes the whole ordered list on standard input and writes it or refuses it as a whole?
open-question.recommendation: One process validates every brief and replaces the file in one atomic write, so the list lands whole and in dependency order or the old file stays byte-for-byte untouched, the Task-derivation commit can never record a partial or reordered plan, and the call keeps one size however many briefs there are; the per-brief forms leave holes or unwritten suffixes behind a refusal, and a separate initialize-then-append leaves a bare heading on disk when the append is refused.
open-question.alternative: Inside the one shell call, derive-tasks runs no separate append. A single initialize process reads the whole ordered list on standard input, in the task file's own ## heading / body / --- form, validates every section, and replaces TASKS_TODO.md with the heading followed by the list in one atomic write. If anything is refused, the file is left byte-for-byte as it was before the run. Append keeps a one-section form only for submit-task's use, if any. The whole derive write is one process and one replace, so no state between the start and the end of the run ever exists on disk: a refusal leaves the old file untouched rather than a bare heading or a partial list, and the call is as short as it can be. Clearing the file and filling it become one subcommand, so derive-tasks no longer exercises an append path, and the tool's initialize contract carries a multi-section stdin format submit-task never uses. A whole-list refusal still means re-sending every brief. What happens to sections already in the file is the initialize-guard question, and this option only works if that answer can be applied in the same call.

Inside the one shell call, derive-tasks runs the initialize call and then one append process per brief, in dependency order, each brief in its own quoted heredoc. Each append runs whether or not the one before it was refused, as each block's embed --recommendation does in the recommendation pass's batch call. A refused brief prints its title with the tool's Error: line while the others land. The append subcommand takes exactly one section on standard input. It copies the per-block shape milestone 44 already proved, a refusal points at one brief, and the tool's stdin contract stays one section per process, the same as submit-task's insert, so derive and submit share one section reader and its tests. A refused brief leaves a hole in the dependency order. Re-sending it with append puts it at the end, after briefs that depend on it, unless the runner switches to a positioned insert. The run's single Task-derivation commit would also pick up a partial list unless the call adds a guard for that. How often this happens depends on how much the tool refuses, which the format-validation and title-uniqueness questions decide. It also needs one heredoc and one process per brief, so the shell call grows with the size of the task list.

alternative.id: Per-brief processes stopping at first refusal

open-question.alternative: Inside the one shell call, derive-tasks runs the initialize call and then one append process per brief, in dependency order, each brief in its own quoted heredoc, chained so the first refusal stops every later append. The task file then holds an ordered prefix. The refused brief is corrected and re-sent together with every brief after it, in order. The append subcommand takes exactly one section on standard input. Dependency order holds whatever is refused: the file is always an ordered prefix of the plan, so a re-send only appends and never needs a positioned insert. The tool still reads one section per process, the same reader submit-task's insert uses, so no multi-section stdin format is needed. A refusal leaves the briefs after it unwritten even when they are valid, so the re-send carries every one of them again. The chained call needs a stop rule and a guard so the commit is skipped or limited while only a prefix has landed, and it still holds one heredoc and one process per brief.

alternative.id: One process for the whole list

open-question.alternative: Inside the one shell call, derive-tasks runs the initialize call and then a single append process. That process reads the whole ordered list on standard input, written as consecutive sections in the task file's own ## heading / body / --- form, and parsed by the same parser the tool uses on the files. It validates every section before it writes anything, then appends all of them in one atomic replace, or refuses the whole list with one Error: line naming the offending section and leaves the file as the initialize call left it. Order and completeness cannot come apart: the list lands whole and in order or not at all, so the one Task-derivation commit never records a partial list. The shell call stays the same size however many briefs there are, and the stdin format is the file format the tool already parses. One bad brief refuses all of them, so a fix re-sends the whole list, and how often that happens depends on how much the tool refuses (the format-validation and title-uniqueness questions). Append now reads several sections on stdin while submit-task's insert reads one, which adds a second stdin shape to specify and test. If the append is refused, the file still holds the heading the initialize call wrote.

open-question.question: When a before or after anchor title names no section in TASKS_TODO.md, does the tool refuse the call with an Error: line so submit-task re-calls with append and prints its one-line advisory itself, or does the tool append the section in that call and print the fallback advisory in the runner's place, breaking the rule that a mutator prints nothing on success?
open-question.recommendation: Position encodes dependency order, so a task must never land anywhere but where the runner decided, and the runner chose its anchor from the file it had just read, which makes a miss a retyping slip that the quoted Error: line fixes on a re-run; the append forms either break the silent-mutator contract or move a prerequisite to the end silently, the flag adds an optional input for one caller, and the re-call form adds a branch on a tool failure to the skill for a fallback that guesses at position.
open-question.alternative: The tool refuses an unknown anchor with one Error: line and the file unchanged, and submit-task drops the append fallback altogether: on that refusal it inserts nothing, commits nothing, and stops, quoting the tool's Error: line verbatim so the user can re-run with a correct anchor. The tool keeps its full output contract. Both the tool contract and the skill stay simple: no second call, no advisory, no tool-side policy, and a task is never placed somewhere other than where the runner decided, which matters because position encodes dependency order. It changes submit-task's documented behaviour, so a slip in the anchor text costs the user a whole re-run of the skill (triage and authoring included) instead of a slightly misplaced task, and a headless chain that runs submit-task stops where today it would continue. How often that happens depends on the title-matching rule the sibling question settles.

The tool refuses an unknown before/after anchor with one Error: line, exit 1, and TASKS_TODO.md byte-for-byte unchanged, exactly like any other failure. submit-task keeps its fallback: on that refusal it makes a second shell call that inserts with append, chained with its commit steps, and prints its one-line advisory itself beside the status line. The tool keeps the full output contract (a mutator prints nothing on success, every failure is one Error: line with nothing written). The tool contract shared with open_questions.py and define_milestone.py stays unchanged, so the contract tests and every caller can rely on one rule: exit 0 means written and silent, exit 1 means nothing written. The fallback policy stays in the one skill that owns it, and a refused insert stops the chained commit through ordinary exit-status chaining. A miss costs a second shell call: the first chained call stops at the refusal and the runner must notice it, re-issue the insert as append, and re-run its commit steps. submit-task's prose then needs a branch on the tool's Error: line, which is the kind of tool-failure handling the batched runners otherwise avoid. How often this path runs depends on the title-matching rule the sibling question settles.

The tool absorbs the fallback: when a before/after anchor names no section, it appends the section at the end of TASKS_TODO.md in the same call, exits 0, and prints one fixed advisory line saying the anchor was not found and the section was appended. submit-task forwards that line as its advisory and runs no second call. This is a deliberate exception to the rule that a mutator prints nothing on success, stated for this one case. The insert and its commit stay one chained shell call on every path, the miss path included, so submit-task's prose carries no branch on a tool failure. The fallback rule is enforced by tested code rather than by the runner remembering to re-call. It breaks the uniform output contract the tools share: "exit 0 and empty output" no longer means a plain success, test_contract.py-style pins need an exception, and any later caller of the insert subcommand (derive-tasks included) inherits a silent change of position unless it reads stdout. The tool also takes over a policy (append rather than stop) that is submit-task's to own.

The tool refuses an unknown anchor by default with one Error: line and the file unchanged. submit-task passes an explicit flag (for example --or-append) that tells the tool to append instead when the anchor names no section; only under that flag does the tool append, exit 0, and print one fixed advisory line, which submit-task forwards. Calls without the flag keep the full silent-on-success contract. The fallback is visible at the call site that wants it, so no caller gets a changed position by default, while submit-task still inserts and commits in one chained call on every path. It adds a flag and a second output mode to the tool for a single caller, so the exception to "a mutator prints nothing on success" still exists, only scoped, and both the default and flagged paths need their own tests. The policy (append on a miss) still moves partly into the tool's interface.

The tool appends the section at the end when a before/after anchor names no section, exits 0, and prints nothing, keeping the mutator output contract intact. The one-line fallback advisory is retired: submit-task reports only its fixed status line, and the actual position is visible only in the committed diff. One chained call on every path with no change to the output contract and no branch in submit-task's prose; since submit-task picks the anchor from the task list it just read, a miss is a rare slip and the commit diff still records where the section landed. It drops the user-visible notice the skill promises today ("say so"), so a mistyped anchor silently puts a prerequisite task at the end of the list, where complete-all-tasks would run it after the tasks that depend on it. The tool also embeds the append-on-miss policy with no trace in its output.
